name: startup-applied-os-sandbox-that-refuses-to-run-unprotected
what: The sandbox seam's contract is that confine() must return enforcing argv or THROW — silent unconfined passthrough is forbidden. exec resolves confinement once at spawn: a confined policy with no provider throws SandboxUnavailableError BEFORE spawning, a capability mismatch throws, and a provider whose runner failed to start (bwrap exit 125 / windows-acl-run exit 127, matched by signature) is translated into SandboxUnavailableError rather than surfaced as an ordinary non-zero exit, because the command body never executed. sandbox-local dispatches on process.platform with three fail-closed arms (win32 without an injected ACL backend, linux without a successful bwrap probe, any other platform) and every arm either confines or throws; no passthrough arm exists. The Linux probe runs a REAL confined 'true' rather than 'bwrap --version' because --version passes on hosts where user namespaces are blocked.
invariants: A policy demanding read isolation on a backend that cannot declare it is REFUSED, never degraded
Both local backends declare capabilities { readIsolation: false } honestly
A confined command never runs unconfined just because a backend is missing
failurePolicy: fail-closed: SandboxUnavailableError carries the message '...refusing to run the command unconfined', SANDBOX_UNAVAILABLE is the stable code string, and the escalation approval path throws when no approval channel is composed

name: confinement-covers-only-shell-fs-fs-search-and-terminal-have-no-sandbox-integration
what: Only the shell tools carry a sandbox policy: ShellToolDeps has an optional sandboxPolicy that is attached to both exec.run and exec.runBackground as the `sandbox` field, and the provider is handed to registerExec which composes the exec service. Everything else is unconfined. packages/fs/src contains ZERO sandbox symbols and FsToolDeps carries only workspace + rewind; the fs 'confinement' is resolvePath's relative-path '..' refusal, while an ABSOLUTE path is taken as-is and may point outside the workspace. fs-search has no sandbox field and calls exec.run with only { argv, cwd }, so ripgrep runs unconfined even under a read-only session mode. terminal has no sandbox parameter on its PTY tools (TerminalToolDeps carries only service + cwd) and no timeoutMs on any terminal_*/process_* tool. The practical consequence of the shell-only wiring: a sandbox refusal inside a shell tool is not caught, so it propagates out of the tool body and the agent records tool/error and discards the whole batch — one refused command fails the entire turn; the background variant instead becomes an errored job.
invariants: Write-path confinement for the fs family is a path check, not OS-level isolation
'A win-ACL sandbox exists' does not imply 'every file operation is confined'
failurePolicy: fail-closed at the shell boundary but with turn-wide cost (the refusal kills the turn rather than degrading); fs/fs-search/terminal have no refusal path at all because they have no policy input

name: read-isolation-is-declared-but-absent-the-gate-is-never-armed-outside-tests
what: No backend declares read isolation. Both local backends declare capabilities { readIsolation: false }; the Linux bwrap profile uses `--ro-bind / /`, so the whole filesystem stays READABLE (writes are isolated, content is not); and the Windows ACL backend's own header states that writes are restricted while reads, network and process visibility are NOT, because WRITE_RESTRICTED intersects only write accesses. The only related mechanism is a refusal gate: assertSandboxCapable throws SandboxUnavailableError when policy.requireReadIsolation === true and the provider does not declare readIsolation:true, and a missing declaration is treated as { readIsolation: false }. Repo-wide, requireReadIsolation is set ONLY by tests (packages/sandbox/test/enforcement.test.ts and packages/exec/test/enforcement.test.ts) and by no src caller, so in composed use the gate is never armed; the in-code comment itself records that every provider is readIsolation:false and the gate is a contract left for future account-style backends.
invariants: Capabilities unknown means NOT read-isolated (fail closed, never fail open)
A demand for read isolation is an opt-in that turns capability absence into a refuse-to-run
failurePolicy: fail-closed by contract, inert in practice: the refusal path exists and is unit-tested but no shipped composition can reach it because nothing sets requireReadIsolation

name: windows-write-restricted-token-backend
what: The Windows backend builds a WRITE_RESTRICTED token whose restricting-SID list is mode-selected: read-only gets [logon SID, EVERYONE] and workspace-write adds the per-workspace write SID plus an optional per-temp write SID; Authenticated Users and INTERACTIVE/LOCAL are deliberately absent from BOTH lists (AU fails the WMI namespace check and standing AU ACEs on the C: root close a tree-creation escape; INTERACTIVE/LOCAL is dropped because the Public tree grants writes to INTERACTIVE). Because read-only carries no write SID, a stale workspace ACE stays inert. Capability identity is split: a deterministic per-workspace SID derived from the canonical workspace path and a domain-separated per-private-temp SID. Grant lifecycle is asymmetric — workspace ACEs are STANDING (the cross-session reuse cache) while temp ACEs are REVOCABLE and removed by dispose() — and grants are idempotent: grantWrite reads the directory's explicit DACL and SKIPS the apply when the exact ACE is already present, under a per-path exclusive LockFileEx lock. Confinement prefixes an argv runner that spawns the child under that token (never unrestricted) and assigns the suspended child to a kill-on-close job before it runs.
invariants: The per-call SandboxPolicy is the enforcement input; the construction options' `mode` is never read by the factory
Every Win32 call is checked; the confined child is never spawned unrestricted; a runner failure exits 127 with a matchable signature
failurePolicy: fail-closed at every level: construction throws on a missing/non-directory writableDir, a grant failure cleans up and rethrows, init() rolls back revocable grants/SIDs/handles before rethrowing, confine() after dispose throws SandboxUnavailableError, dispose() reports every cleanup failure as AggregateError

name: sandbox-escalation-ladder-declared-tested-no-production-caller
what: A strictly-wider escalation ladder exists in the seam: WIDER_MODES maps read-only -> [workspace-write, danger-full-access] and workspace-write -> [danger-full-access]; approveEscalation rejects a non-wider target, a missing approver and a missing agent, and maps outcome rejected/cancelled/unavailable to distinct errors; sandboxDenialMarker and escalationHintMarker render tool-output TEXT markers (not SessionEvents) and validateEscalationArgs checks the advertised argument shape. Repo-wide the entire surface appears in production src only at its definition and re-export — the only other references are the package's own tests — and NO tool schema declares the `sandbox_permissions` / `justification` parameters that the marker text advertises, so the ladder does not exist on any production path. writableRoots() and canonicalPath() are likewise test-only in composed use; writableRoots is nonetheless the single home of the workspace-write meaning (workspaceRoot + /tmp + tmpdir(), canonicalized and deduped) so the profile dialects and any in-process fence cannot drift apart.
invariants: Escalation is strictly-wider and checked at execution time, never baked into a tool schema
failurePolicy: fail-closed: approveEscalation throws when no approval service/channel is composed; but the whole path is unreachable in production

constants.name: writableRoots (workspace-write)
constants.value: workspaceRoot + '/tmp' + tmpdir(), canonicalized and deduped; read-only => []

name: sandbox-mode-resolution-and-advisory-prompt-text
what: The effective sandbox mode for a session is resolved request.mode > the session's LAST sandbox/mode event (the scan runs backwards, last-writer-wins) > the configured default ('read-only'), then path.resolve on the workspace root. The rendered policy text is injected into the system prompt and is explicitly ADVISORY: it tells the model not to refuse a required modification from the policy alone but to try an available tool normally and follow any denial/escalation guidance it returns. The resolved policy object is passed to BOTH the enforcer and this renderer so they cannot drift.
invariants: A mode change is a log append; there is no separate mutable mode field
The same resolved policy feeds enforcement and the prompt text
failurePolicy: no enforcement here (pure resolution): an unrecognized mode falls through to the default arm and renders an empty string

name: three-layer-approval-policy-with-an-advisory-danger-classifier
what: The approval policy has three layers as implemented: a readOnly tool is allowed; a `write` with no path or a path outside the workspace asks; any other non-readOnly tool asks (layer-1 fallback); EXCEPT bash/pwsh, which ask ONLY when classifyDanger() != 'none' — a benign registered shell command therefore executes with NO approval even with askForNonReadOnly true and no answerer. For the shell tools the safety boundary IS the classifier, and it is advisory: it parses the tool's own getArgv output, and the file records the bypass surface it is meant to survive (quoted 'r''m', metachar '; rm -rf /', and control flow whose every basename is harmless). Deny-on-metachar treats any argv token containing one of 7 metachars (the array is [";", "&&", "|", "$(", "`", ">", "<"]; a '>>' token is caught by the ">" membership test rather than being a separate element) as dangerous even when every basename looks harmless, and a force-delete is 'extreme' only when its targets lie outside the workspace or name a top-level system path. approvalPolicy 'never' promotes an ask-decision into deny-with-reason instead of consulting the answerer, and the policy seeds BOTH a plain listener and a waterfall handler from one shared decide() because a waterfall-only handler is invisible to ctx.resolveDecision.
invariants: Over-asking is the intended direction at the metachar layer: it is deliberately deny-on-metachar, not a precise effect model
A returned decision object must not be able to short-circuit an ancestor guard (the handler returns undefined rather than {kind:'allow'})
failurePolicy: mixed and explicitly tiered: an unknown tool asks (fail closed); 'no applicable decision' is undefined = allow, which for a benign shell command is deliberate fail-open; 'never' turns every ask into deny

name: guardian-auto-review-subagent-with-fail-closed-verdict-and-breaker
what: An optional LLM approval guardian spawns a dedicated no-tools 'reviewer' role via spawnChild with forkTurns 'none' (reclaimed in finally) and requires a strict-JSON verdict; only 'allow' falls through to the human answerer, while deny, timeout and malformed all DENY. Deny, timeout and malformed are all counted by a circuit breaker over the last 10 reviews at 3 non-allow outcomes, and the breaker has a durable mirror whose read failure yields a fresh CLOSED breaker (fail-soft on persistence). The reviewer's context is bounded (transcript maxChars 4000 / maxEvents 12, per-line slice 200).
invariants: A timeout or malformed verdict is treated as the stuck-reviewer failure the breaker exists for, not as model disagreement
Only an explicit allow reaches the human
failurePolicy: fail-closed deny on open breaker, timeout (cause:'timeout'), malformed JSON (cause:'malformed'), a missing reviewer entry and missing final text; the durable breaker mirror is fail-soft

name: hooks-as-fail-closed-gates-and-fail-visible-observers
what: User-configured hook handlers are spawned as subprocesses (no shell) with the HookContext as one JSON object on stdin, must emit exactly one JSON HookOutput object on stdout, are killed after timeoutMs and have stdout/stderr capped. The event list is exactly 9 events and each is classified as GATE or OBSERVER: pre-tool/post-tool, prompt/submit, stop and permission are gates (deny/ask, block:true, continue:false, a handler error, a non-zero exit, a timeout, unparseable stdout and a trust mismatch ALL become HookBlockedError), while session/start, session/end, subagent/stop and notification are observers where a trust failure or handler error is reported and skipped. Handler type (command | mcpTool | prompt | agent) only TAGS a handler for trust/audit in v1 — every handler is executed as `command.cmd args`. Per-run hash trust is a security boundary: the executed artifact's sha256 is recomputed on EVERY invocation and compared with the configured value. Config loading is strict about shape but distinguishes an EXPLICIT configPath (missing -> HookConfigError) from the default path (missing -> zero handlers). WIRING: createHookRegistry has ZERO non-test callers (every call site is packages/hooks/test/hooks.test.ts), so although the gate/observer semantics, the per-invocation trust hashing and the output validation are fully implemented and unit-tested, no shipped host mounts them: the only shipped consumer of this package is the TUI's read-only inventory panel (packages/tui/src/app/slash/impl/eco.ts:17 imports resolveHooksConfigPath/loadHooksConfig/HOOK_EVENTS, used at :72-85, rendered by packages/tui/src/views/light-hooks.ts:5). The gate layer is therefore an unconnected seam, not an active safety control.
invariants: A gate fails closed on every failure class; an observer never becomes fatal
ask is not wired to a question seam on main, so a permission 'ask' is a fail-closed DENY in v1
failurePolicy: fail-closed for gates, fail-open-but-visible for observers

constants.name: HOOK_EVENTS
constants.value: 9: session/start, session/end, prompt/submit, pre-tool, post-tool, permission, stop, subagent/stop, notification

name: agent-preset-as-scoped-per-agent-configuration
what: A preset is a validated JSON shape (name/systemPrompt/tools/model) whose tools are resolved EVERY one BEFORE any scope mutation, so an unknown tool throws with no partial mount, and the resolved tools plus a 'preset' service go into a freshly mounted CHILD scope (lazily creating a tools/registry when the caller exposed none) so a preset cannot leak its tools or prompt into the parent. The I-harness-owned DEFAULT_AGENT_PRESET system prompt is the readable in-repo source and is treated as a BASE by the assembly — the assembly composes its runtime sections AFTER it and appends the sandbox policy context, while the user message always outranks the system prompt.
invariants: Resolution happens before any scope mutation (no half-mounted child)
The default prompt is a base, not the final prompt
failurePolicy: fail-loud: parsePreset throws on a missing name/systemPrompt/tools and mountPreset throws on an unknown tool before any scope mutation

name: repeat-call-nudge-guard-observational-never-blocking
what: Counts consecutive identical tool calls by the key name + JSON.stringify(args) per Session (state in a WeakMap keyed by the Session object, so entries are GC'd with their session) and, at each configured threshold in a LIST (default [3,5,8]), appends an internal user/message nudge telling the model to consider changing approach. Any different key resets the counter to 1. Misconfiguration fails loud at construction (thresholds must be a non-empty array of integers >= 2).
invariants: Only an unbroken run of identical calls counts as a loop
The nudge is an internal message (internal:true, plugin source), not a user turn
failurePolicy: observational — no deny or escalation path; only a message append

name: tool-timeout-guard-converting-a-hang-into-tool-timeout
what: A cascade handler on tools/execute enforces the TOOL's declared timeoutMs by swapping in a linked AbortController and, when its OWN timer fired, substituting {error, code:'TOOL_TIMEOUT'} at the TOP level of the raw value (spreading the tool's other fields) so it reads at tool/result.output.code. The guard's own timeout is distinguished from an upstream (parent) cancel by a local timedOut flag; the derived controller is linked to the upstream signal and unlinked in finally, and a tool that honors the abort by REJECTING still surfaces TOOL_TIMEOUT instead of propagating the rejection. The guard holds NO default: with no timeoutMs the call is unbounded, and the config object is an empty placeholder reserved for future knobs.
invariants: Per-tool policy stays with the tool; the guard has no hardcoded tunables
A parent cancel is not a timeout
failurePolicy: converts a hang into a structured failure value rather than a throw

name: tool-retry-guard-with-re-entrancy-protection
what: A cascade handler re-dispatches a tool call whose result carries TOOL_TIMEOUT, with exponential backoff + jitter and a retry cap. Mount order is load-bearing: this guard must be registered BEFORE the timeout guard so it stays OUTER and sees the raw TOOL_TIMEOUT, and the ORIGINAL caller signal is captured before the inner timeout guard swaps exec.abortSignal (after a TOOL_TIMEOUT that controller is aborted, so reading the signal later would falsely stop retrying). Re-dispatch deliberately bypasses the registry's pre-execute hooks, the monotonic guards and post-execute — approval was already granted — and marks the frame with markCascadeRedispatch so once-per-logical-call cascade handlers (hooks pre/post-tool) skip their own run. A WeakSet of in-flight dispatch objects guards re-entrancy: a nested frame delegates to next() instead of retrying, because re-invoking the cascade would otherwise multiply attempts exponentially.
invariants: Only TOOL_TIMEOUT triggers a retry
A retry frame is not a new logical call (the redispatch marker)
failurePolicy: bounded best-effort recovery: after maxRetries the last timeout result is returned unchanged; an upstream abort during backoff stops retrying
